title: The Princes in the Tower
subtitle: Tower of London · 1483
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: The Tower of London, fourteen eighty-three. Two brothers were lodged inside: Edward, twelve, already proclaimed king, and Richard, nine.
beats.picture: PAINTING by Paul Delaroche, "Edward V and the Duke of York in the Tower", 1831 (Wallace Collection): the two boys sitting close on a great curtained bed, one holding a book, a small dog looking toward the door.

beats.vo: Through that summer, the boys were seen less and less behind these walls. Then not at all.
beats.picture: Photochrom print of the Tower of London, about 1890-1900 (Library of Congress): the White Tower rising behind the outer walls, trees, a road with carriages in front.

beats.vo: Their uncle had taken the throne, as Richard the Third, painted here a century later.
beats.picture: Portrait of Richard III, late 16th century, National Portrait Gallery, London (painted about a century after his death; inscription RICARDVS III ANG REX).

beats.vo: In sixteen seventy-four, workmen at the Tower found the bones of two children under a staircase. Charles the Second had them laid in Westminster Abbey.
beats.picture: Photochrom print of Westminster Abbey, about 1890-1900 (Library of Congress).

beats.vo: The bones were examined in nineteen thirty-three, and never DNA tested. These faces are a painter's guess.
beats.picture: PAINTING by John Everett Millais, "The Princes in the Tower", 1878: the two boys in black standing together at the foot of a dark stair.

facts.claim: In 1483 Edward V (born 2 Nov 1470, so 12) and his brother Richard, Duke of York (born 17 Aug 1473, so 9 when he joined him in June 1483) were lodged in the Tower of London; Edward had been proclaimed king on his father's death (9 April 1483) and was never crowned
Their uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, took the throne as Richard III after Edward was declared deposed on 25 June 1483
The boys were seen less and less (Mancini: withdrawn into the inner apartments, seen behind bars and windows) and there are no recorded sightings of either after the summer of 1483

In 1674 workmen at the Tower found the bones of two children under a staircase (the Abbey says 'under a staircase in the White Tower'; HRP notes the exact spot is debated, so the film says only 'at the Tower')

The bones were brought to Westminster Abbey by order of Charles II and placed in a white marble urn designed by Christopher Wren (Latin inscription dated 1678; film gives no urn year because sources differ)
The urn was opened and the bones examined in July 1933 (Tanner, Wright, Northcroft); remaining bones were of two young children; sex was not established
The bones have never been DNA tested; requests to disturb them were refused (Elizabeth II never granted approval); whose they are has not been proven

Still unresolved as of 2026: Feb 2025 National Geographic says only that King Charles 'could' allow a new investigation; March 2026 coverage still treats the bones as contested and untested; no test or identification reported

B01 is Paul Delaroche's painting 'Edward V and the Duke of York in the Tower', 1831, Wallace Collection; B05 is Millais's 'The Princes in the Tower', 1878 (Royal Holloway) — both imagined scenes, hence 'these faces are a painter's guess'
B03 is the NPG 148 portrait of Richard III, unknown artist, late 16th century (about a century after his death in 1485)
